rashi:a1.1: Unless he was an expert like Ila: who lived in Yavne, who was pious and was not suspected of this.
rashi:a1.2: Whether [unblemished or blemished]: [whether or not] he told them it was a permanent blemish, he would regularly take his full wage.
gershom:a1.1: Like Ila: whom they permitted [to take a wage] because of his effort.
rashi:a2.1: Gemara. What is the reason: [that he takes] four issar for a small animal and six for a large one?
gershom:a2.1: What is the reason: [that he takes] four for a small animal and six for a large one?
rashi:a2.2: A large animal involves great effort: throwing it to the ground, binding it and looking at its blemish.
gershom:a3.1: This one: a large animal involves great effort to examine.
rashi:a3.1: But an unblemished one: when he tells them it is a temporary blemish, why does he take a wage? It does him [the owner] no good, since he is forbidding it.
rashi:a3.2: That if so: that he would not take a wage [for an unblemished animal], people would come to suspect him when he says it is blemished.
gershom:a4.1: That if so: [this is why] Ila takes a wage for an unblemished one too.
gershom:a5.1: They would come to suspect him: [of declaring it unblemished] so that he could take a wage for it another time, when it again develops another blemish.
rashi:a4.1: They did not institute it for him twice: for when he says it is unblemished he takes his wage, and when they bring it before him several more times he takes nothing; therefore there is no suspicion.
tosafot:a4.1: They did not institute it for him twice: And if you say: people will still say that this one is unblemished, and the reason he permitted it is that he does not want to take the trouble another time. One can say: the Sages did not obligate him to examine it another time; they said only that if he does examine it, he cannot take a wage for it. Furthermore, in this matter people would never suspect him of permitting a prohibition in order to spare himself the trouble of a second time.
gershom:a6.1: Twice: they did not institute for him to take a wage twice for one animal, and so people will not come to suspect him.
tosafot:a5.1: One who takes his wages to judge, his rulings are void: As for what we learned in a mishna, “Ugly is the judge who takes a wage to judge, but his ruling is a ruling,” it is explained in the last chapter of Ketubot (105a) as referring to compensation for idleness that is evident, which is permitted.
rashi:a5.1: Mishna. To sprinkle: the water of purification.
rashi:a5.2: To sanctify: to put the ashes of purification together with living water in a vessel.
gershom:a7.1: And to sanctify: to put water onto the ashes of purification.
rashi:a5.3: Burnt ashes: like any other ordinary ashes. All ash is called burnt ashes [efer miklah].
rashi:a5.4: [The next clause means:] But if that examiner of firstborns, or the judge, or the witness, or the one who sprinkles or the one who sanctifies, was a priest, and the one who takes him along leads him through a place of impurity because there is no other way.
gershom:a8.1: If he was a priest: the judge or the witness.
rashi:a6.1: Renders him impure from his teruma: and causes him a loss, since he must buy non-sacred food to eat, and non-sacred produce costs more than teruma, because non-sacred food is fit for everyone while teruma is fit only for priests.
gershom:a9.1: And renders him impure from his teruma: he takes him to his town, and on the way there is impurity, and he leads him through it and renders him impure, and prevents him from eating teruma. He suffers a loss by this: had he been pure he would eat teruma, whose price is low, and now he must buy non-sacred food, which is expensive. Since he causes him this loss, he must feed him, give him drink and smear him with oil, and this payment is permitted.
rashi:a6.2: He feeds him: the one who takes him along [gives him food], drink, and oil to smear.
rashi:a6.3: And he gives him his wage like a laborer: the Gemara explains what this is: he gives him according to what he causes him to lose.
rashi:a7.1: Gemara. From where are these matters derived: that one does not take a wage for issuing a ruling, or for Torah that one teaches?
tosafot:a7.1: Just as I did so for free…: And if you say: why then do I need “And you shall take no bribe,” which the Merciful One wrote (Exodus 23:8)? This is no refutation, for they are two separate matters, as is evident at the beginning of the last chapter of Ketubot (105a): taking it as a wage means payment for his trouble, and taking it as a bribe means [payment] so that he will make an effort to judge him well and turn the case in his favor, as it says there: even to acquit the innocent and to convict the guilty. Nor should one wonder about the judges of decrees in Jerusalem, who took their wages from the collection of the Temple chamber: even without the reason of evident compensation for idleness, it was permitted there, since all their occupation was this and they engaged in no other work, so that they necessarily had to be supported. And as for the current practice of teaching Torah for a wage: if he has nothing to live on, it is permitted; and even if he does, if it is evident compensation for idleness, in that he leaves all his business and dealings, it stands to reason that this counts as more evident than [the case of] Karna, who would smell wine and take money [Ketubot 105a]. Furthermore, with children it is permitted on account of supervising them, and as payment for teaching the cantillation marks, as is evident in the chapter Ein Bein HaMudar (Nedarim 37a).
gershom:a10.1: One who betroths: a woman with the water of purification or the ashes of purification. Evidently one may benefit from them.
rashi:a9.1: She is betrothed: evidently he may take payment [for them], for otherwise with what would he be betrothing them?
rashi:a9.2: Even though he is an Israelite: even if this man is an Israelite; [this is stated] because priests are the ones accustomed to sprinkling and sanctifying.
tosafot:a9.1: One who betroths with the water of purification or the ashes of purification, she is betrothed, even though he is an Israelite: Rashi’s explanation, that it states “even though he is an Israelite” because priests are accustomed to sprinkling and sanctifying, is forced. The Ri says that it states this mainly because of the first clause, as it teaches in the first clause in the second chapter of Kiddushin (58a): One who betroths with teruma, with tithes, with the priestly gifts, with the water of purification or with the ashes of purification… [“even though he is an Israelite” belongs to that whole list].
rashi:a10.1: Payment: for bringing the ashes, that he goes from a distant place to Jerusalem to bring the ashes.
rashi:a10.2: And payment for filling: the water; he may take this, since he takes payment for his trouble and not for the act that makes the mitzva valid.
gershom:a11.1: With the payment for bringing water and filling: he may betroth.
rashi:a10.3: Here, payment for sprinkling and sanctifying: which is itself what makes the mitzva valid; [for this] he may not take [payment].
gershom:a12.1: With the payment for sprinkling and sanctifying: no.
rashi:a11.1: With the water of purification: which implies filling the water; and “with the ashes” can be explained as bringing the ashes.
rashi:a12.1: How does he go: he is violating “None shall render himself impure for the dead” (Leviticus 21:1).
gershom:a13.1: He himself: the priest, how can he go to a place of impurity? He is violating a prohibition.
rashi:a13.1: To a beit haperas: which he is not admonished against walking through.
rashi:a13.2: As Rav Yehuda says: A person may blow on a beit haperas and walk: since a bone the size of a barley grain imparts impurity by contact and by carrying but not by overhang, when he blows on it, it is pushed away before him and he does not touch it. However, he may not eat teruma, as we say in Ḥagiga, in the chapter Ḥomer BaKodesh (Ḥagiga 25b): one examines for those performing the Paschal offering, but one does not examine for those eating teruma; and that “one examines” is explained there as referring to this examination of a beit haperas.
gershom:a14.1: A person may blow on a beit haperas and walk: this applies to those performing the Paschal offering, since [the Sages] did not uphold their words where karet is at stake; but with regard to teruma they upheld their words, and he becomes impure.
tosafot:a13.1: In brief: The Gemara implies that by blowing he may go [through a beit haperas] to testify, yet he is still impure, as the mishna says “renders him impure from his teruma.” This is difficult for Rabbeinu Tam, who holds that blowing helps for everything. His reason: in Pesaḥim (92a) a mishna of Oholot (18:4) is cited, “one examines for those performing the Paschal offering but not for those eating teruma,” and the Gemara asks “What is ‘examines’?” and answers with Rav Yehuda’s blowing; but the mishna itself explains the examination (sifting the earth in a fine sieve for a bone the size of a barley grain), and blowing helps for other matters too, as in Eiruvin (30b), for a priest in a cemetery. So Rabbeinu Tam deletes “What is ‘examines’?”: Rav Yehuda’s blowing is a separate rule that helps for everything, while the mishna’s sifting helps only for the Paschal offering. On his view, our mishna’s priest became impure because he walked without blowing, and Rav Yehuda is cited only to show that the beit haperas is rabbinic, as Rashi explained in Ketubot (28b). But then it would be permitted without blowing for every mitzva, which is hard to square with Eiruvin (47a), which lists only Torah study, marriage, going to court and contesting among gentiles (compare Megilla 27a and, for human dignity, Berakhot 19b). Tosafot answer that the same may apply to every mitzva, and discuss the She’iltot of Rav Aḥai, who permits it for every mitzva, such as greeting kings, and the puzzle of walking with a mourner through a beit haperas (Berakhot) if one must blow at every step. Tosafot’s teacher objects to Rabbeinu Tam from Ḥagiga (25b), where the Gemara clearly inserts Rav Yehuda’s statement as the explanation of the mishna, so the words “What is ‘examines’?” must be read. He explains: the mishna’s sifting is done after one has passed through, for every purpose, while “examines” means beforehand, in order to pass through for the Paschal offering. There are then three categories: for the Paschal offering (and a nazirite, for Beit Shammai), he blows and is pure; for Torah study, marriage, going to court and human dignity, he may even enter without blowing; for other mitzvot, like the testimony here, he may enter by blowing but remains impure. The case of the eiruv is resolved accordingly (Eiruvin 82a), and the question in Ḥagiga (25b) about one who examined for his Paschal offering eating teruma refers to Rav Yehuda’s examination. Alternatively, all the examinations are for the Paschal offering, and Rav Yehuda explains “what is ‘examines’” beforehand, in the style of Bava Metzia 21a and Bava Batra 22b. rashi:b1.1: A beit haperas that has been trodden: that people have trodden with their feet, is pure, since a bone the size of a barley grain cannot avoid being crushed underfoot; and a beit haperas carries no uncertainty except because of a bone the size of a barley grain, since a beit haperas is a field in which a grave was plowed.
tosafot:b1.1: And Rav Yehuda bar Ami said in the name of Rav Yehuda: A beit haperas that has been trodden is pure: In the last chapter of Ḥagiga (25a) the reading is: Rav Ḥiyya, son of Rabbi Ami, in the name of Ulla.
gershom:b1.1: That has been trodden is pure: with regard to those performing the Paschal offering.
rashi:b2.1: Alternatively, with other impurity: he rendered this priest impure, for example with animal carcasses and creeping animals, which he is not admonished against touching.
gershom:b2.1: Alternatively, with other impurities: such as animal carcasses and creeping animals, since [priests] are admonished only about the impurity of a corpse.
rashi:b3.1: Like an idle laborer of that same labor: from which he is kept idle. If he was a pearl driller, whose work is easy to do and whose pay is high, and one says to him: Take such-and-such and be idle from work today, he reduces his pay only slightly, since it is easy and involves no effort. And if it is hard work, like a carpenter: if one says to him, You now take three zuz; take one zuz, be idle today from that work, and do this easy work, he will gladly be idle and take a zuz. Here too he gives him that sort of wage, since he keeps him from his work; but he does not give him the whole wage, since he is not engaged in hard work for him.
gershom:b3.1: Like an idle laborer of that same labor from which he is idle: for the matter can go toward leniency or stringency. How so? A tailor or a scribe, whose work involves little effort, earns three [coins] a day. Plainly, if someone hires him on condition that he be idle from his work and guard his house, and asks him to forgo some of his wage since he is idle and not exerting himself, then since his craft is without effort he will be willing to forgo only a little of his wage, say one small coin. But a laborer whose work is hard, such as a porter, will surely gladly forgo half his wage or more on condition that he be idle. Here too, he gives the judge or the witness his wage according to the craft from which he keeps him idle.
tosafot:b3.1: In brief: Rashi explained that “an idle laborer of that same labor” is paid what he would accept to give up his own work and do this easier task: a pearl driller, whose work is easy and well paid, would give up little; a carpenter, earning three zuz at hard work, would gladly take one zuz to be idle and do something easy. Tosafot object: if he is paid for leaving his work to do this task, he is being paid to judge, to testify, to sprinkle and to sanctify. Rather, he is paid what he would accept to be idle from his own work altogether, doing nothing. The same must be said in Bava Metzia (31b) about one who returns a lost item, “he gives him his wage like an idle laborer,” where Rashi explained as here; otherwise he would be taking a wage for returning a lost item, against the view that a guardian of a lost item is an unpaid guardian (Bava Kamma 56b). Rabbeinu Ḥananel explained there that one who now earns a sela for sewing a garment at festival time is paid only the half sela he would earn the rest of the year; Tosafot find this puzzling, since the wording does not suggest it and it has no reason. And in Bava Metzia (76b), on workers who came and found the field wet, “one who does work is not like one who sits idle,” and Rav cited Ḥavivi as saying that he would have paid “like an idle laborer”: this means one who is completely idle, not as Rashi or Rabbeinu Ḥananel explained. A difficulty remains from Bava Metzia (68a), on setting up a shopkeeper for half the profit only if one pays him “like an idle laborer,” which the Gemara there explains as “of that same labor from which he is idle,” adding that the clause about one who toils was needed; and from the baraita and Tosefta there in which Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon dispute how much he is paid. On Rashi’s explanation these are difficult, but on Tosafot’s they fit: Rabbi Meir’s “whether much or little” refers to whether his own work was heavy or light, and Rabbi Shimon’s “his full wage” is what he would accept to leave heavy work for this kind of work, which is more than Rabbi Meir’s; and the Tosefta’s “one who sits idle” means idle from that heavier work. Rabbeinu Ḥananel there explained “an idle laborer” as one who cannot find work and would hire himself out cheaply, rather than at the high current rate. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:b4.1: Mishna. One who is suspect with regard to firstborn animals: for example, suspected of inflicting a blemish on a firstborn.
rashi:b4.2: Deer meat: since it is red, it can be confused with calf meat; sometimes he sells an unblemished firstborn calf and says it is deer meat.
gershom:b4.1: Nor hides that are not tanned: since they may be from a firstborn.
rashi:b4.3: Of a female: since there is no concern of firstborn status.
gershom:b5.1: But one may purchase hides of a female from him: since a female is not sanctified as a firstborn.
rashi:b4.4: But one may purchase spun thread and garments from him: since if it were from a firstborn he would not have taken the trouble over them, as he is careful about his effort.
gershom:b6.1: Since it can be confused with that of a calf: since its meat is red.
rashi:b6.1: Gemara. The Sages will hear: that it is an unblemished firstborn and requires burial, and they will cause me a loss; and he is careful about his effort and does not tan them.
gershom:b7.1: He thinks: If I tan it and afterward it becomes known that it is from a firstborn and they forbid it to me, I will have lost my effort. Therefore, when it is tanned, it is known that it is not from a firstborn; and if it is not tanned, we are concerned.
rashi:b7.1: It is known: [the difference] between a male’s hide and a female’s hide.
gershom:b8.1: It is known: since they have no place of a male organ, they are certainly of a female.
rashi:b8.1: He severs: he cuts away its male organ and makes it look like a female’s; and when he is asked, What is this cut in the place where a female’s would be?, he says: Mice ate it.
rashi:b9.1: Dirty [tzo’i]: wool that has not been cleaned of its dirt.
gershom:b9.1: And dirty: that is not bleached.
rashi:b9.2: Now, bleached: of which one could say that he would not waste his effort and would not bleach it, since he thinks the Sages will hear and cause me a loss; even so, since it is a small effort he is not careful about it, and we do not buy it. Is it necessary [to say] dirty?
gershom:b10.1: Now, bleached wool we do not buy: even though one could say that he would not have troubled to bleach it unless it were non-sacred, even so one does not buy it.
gershom:b11.1: Wool bleached from its dirt: but not bleached as fully as it needs.
rashi:b10.1: But one may purchase spun thread and garments from him: since if it were from a firstborn he would not have taken the trouble over them, as he is careful about his effort.
gershom:b12.1: But one may purchase spun thread and garments: since he certainly would not do so much extra work if it were from a firstborn.
rashi:b10.2: Is it necessary [to state] garments: from the moment they were spun they were already permitted.
rashi:b10.3: Felt [namtei]: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), which were never spun; that is why it had to teach it.
gershom:b13.1: What are garments? Not actually woven, but felt [namtei] (Rabbeinu Gershom adds a vernacular gloss), which is easy to make.
rashi:b11.1: Mishna. One who is suspect with regard to the Sabbatical Year: of sowing, or of doing business with aftergrowths.
rashi:b11.2: Combed [serak]: beaten and prepared with a comb.
gershom:b14.1: Even combed: since here one cannot say he would not trouble to comb it, as it is a light matter.
rashi:b12.1: Gemara. Is it necessary [to state] woven: it already reached the stage of spun thread beforehand, and from that moment it was permitted.
rashi:b12.2: Chains [tikhei]: chains, which are called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss); they make them from flax before it is spun.
gershom:b15.1: Tikhei, [that is,] nekili: (Rabbeinu Gershom adds a vernacular gloss), made to resemble spinning.
rashi:b13.1: Mishna. Even water and salt: as a penalty.
rashi:b13.2: Relevance [zikat] to teruma: anything from which teruma is given.
rashi:b14.1: Gemara. For they mix olive oil into them: and since they have relevance to teruma, we do not buy them from him.
gershom:b16.1: For they mix olive oil into them: since oil is obligated in teruma.
